content: 1. Grants from UNICEF, BMGF, and WHO were provided to support work on immunization program performance assessment, recording/reporting, and home-based records. It was determined that these grants did not present a conflict of interest nor influence the recommendations' outcomes. However, as some grants were directly related to home-based records, it was recommended that the funding be declared at the meeting's opening for transparency. 2. WHO recommendations on home-based records for maternal, newborn, and child health were developed with contributions from experts. Declarations of interest and conflict of interest management were as follows: Adolphus Clarke: Expertise in end-user and implementer roles; no conflicts declared. Bandana Das: Expertise in end-user and implementer roles; no conflicts declared. Ilgi Ertem: Expertise in newborn and child health research; no conflicts declared. Hiranya Senani Jayawickrama: Expertise in end-user and implementer roles; received research support from the Australian government for infant feeding research. This was assessed as not presenting a conflict of interest or influencing recommendations. Lydia Karimurio: Expertise in end-user and implementer roles; no conflicts declared. Rintaro Mori: Expertise in women and child health research; no conflicts declared. Kirana Pritasari: Expertise in end-user and implementer roles; no conflicts declared. Maria Ximena Rojas Reyes: Expertise in maternal and newborn health research; no conflicts declared. Jesca Nsungwa Sabiiti: Expertise in end-user and implementer roles; no conflicts declared. Lora Shimp: Expertise in maternal and child health; received research support from BMGF for work on home-based record design and improvement. This was assessed as not presenting a conflict of interest or influencing recommendations. However, it was recommended that the funding be declared at the meeting's opening for transparency. 3. Studies on the use of home-based records for maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) outcomes reported the following: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Norway (Bjerkeli Grøvdal, Grimsmo & Nilsen, 2009) found little or no difference in parents' knowledge of child health over one year between those with a parent-held child health record and those without. An RCT in rural Indonesia (Osaki et al., 2018) found increased knowledge among women in both the intervention group (receiving the MCH handbook) and the control group (sporadic availability of the handbook) regarding maternal and newborn danger signs, birth preparedness, and child sickness prevention and care. However, no significance test between groups was provided. 4. No studies were found on the intensity of use of home-based records or the use of different types of home-based records. 5. A non-RCT in Cambodia (Yanagisawa et al., 2015) found increased maternal knowledge of danger signs during pregnancy and delivery, as well as prevention of anemia, parasite transmission, and mother-to-child HIV transmission. However, no significance test was conducted. 6. Maternal outcomes related to antenatal care (ANC) visits showed mixed results: Two RCTs (955 women) suggested unclear effects on the average number of ANC visits for women with MCH handbooks compared to those without home-based records. Two cluster RCTs reported varying effects on achieving six or more ANC visits, with moderate-certainty evidence. One study (Osaki et al., 2018) reported more care-seeking for pregnancy complications in the intervention area compared to the control area, but this was not statistically significant (very low-certainty evidence). 7. No studies reported on postpartum care visits, postpartum family planning, or maternal immunization. 8. Knowledge outcomes related to home-based records are detailed in Annex 4. 9. For newborn outcomes, no studies reported on care-seeking for newborn illness, postnatal care visits, or newborn warmth and hygiene. 10. Child health care practices, including infant and young child feeding, illness management, growth monitoring, and development monitoring, were not reported in any studies. 11. Communication within households and child mortality/morbidity outcomes were not reported in any studies. 12. Health service outcomes related to the use of home-based records were as follows: An RCT in Norway (Bjerkeli Grøvdal, Grimsmo & Nilsen, 2006) found little or no difference in parents' difficulty communicating with health personnel between those with a parent-held child health record and those without. Another RCT in Norway (Bjerkeli Grøvdal, Grimsmo & Nilsen, 2006) found no difference in parents' satisfaction with information provided about child health between the intervention and control groups. 13. No studies were found on the continuity of care or the use of different types of home-based records to improve health service outcomes. 14. An RCT in Australia (Homer, Davis & Everitt, 1999) found that both intervention (full pregnancy case notes) and control (abbreviated cooperation card) groups of women were positive about their experiences. Women in the intervention group reported a sense of control during antenatal visits. However, no significant differences were found between groups.
